accroche: In 2011, a macaque presses the shutter of an unattended camera. Neither he nor the photographer who set it up holds the copyright.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 2011, British wildlife photographer David Slater sets up his camera on a tripod in the Tangkoko reserve, on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, rigged to photograph crested macaques, a species then critically endangered. He sets the focus, burst mode, and a flash, then steps away. One of the macaques seizes the camera and, in about thirty minutes, presses the shutter hundreds of times. A handful of images are sharp and well framed, including one that shows the monkey with its mouth open, like a broad smile facing the lens.

Published starting on July 4, 2011, the photos go viral. On July 9, one of them is uploaded to Wikimedia Commons labeled “public domain,” a contributor having judged that no human being pressed the shutter and that no one, therefore, holds the copyright. Slater objects and asks for its removal, in vain: Wikimedia refuses, opening a public debate that American law will soon settle twice.

## Neither one nor the other

On December 22, 2014, the date the third edition of its Compendium of Practices takes effect, the U.S. Copyright Office states in black and white that it will register only works created by a human being, and that it will refuse those produced by nature, an animal, or a plant, citing as its very first example a photograph taken by a monkey.

A year later, on September 22, 2015, the animal rights group PETA files suit on behalf of the macaque, whom it names Naruto, as “next friend” authorized to act for him. It asks that ownership of the copyright be recognized as his, with the revenue to fund his protection and that of his habitat. Federal judge William Orrick dismisses the suit on January 28, 2016. PETA appeals.

On April 23, 2018, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirms the dismissal, in an opinion written by Judge Carlos Bea. The reasoning separates two questions: Naruto does have standing under the Constitution, since the complaint alleges a concrete and particularized economic injury; but he lacks standing under the Copyright Act, which does not explicitly authorize any animal to sue. Bea's opinion also awards attorney's fees to Slater, noting that Naruto was left out of an agreement reached seven months earlier, on September 11, 2017, between Slater and PETA, an agreement that provided, in the terms made public by PETA, that 25% of future revenue from the photos would fund macaque protection work. In a separate opinion, Judge N.R. Smith goes further: he faults PETA for having dropped the complaint's original claims along the way and for turning Naruto into an instrument of its own cause rather than a plaintiff it genuinely represented.

## A copyright with no one behind it

The ruling does not say that Slater owns the copyright; it says only that the monkey cannot claim it. The most widely reproduced photo of the dispute remains, to this day, without an author recognized by any court. In 2023, when the Copyright Office examines Zarya of the Dawn, the first graphic novel assisted by generative artificial intelligence to seek registration, it refuses protection for the images themselves, relying on this same requirement, set nine years earlier because of a monkey: without a human hand behind the result, there is no one to whom it can be attributed.

citation.texte: If Congress and the President intended to take the extraordinary step of authorizing animals as well as people and legal entities to sue, they could, and should, have said so plainly.
citation.auteur: the federal district court, in Citizens to End Animal Suffering & Exploitation, Inc. v. New England Aquarium

carte.punch: A selfie taken by a monkey belongs neither to the monkey nor to the photographer who set up the camera.
carte.idee: In 2011, a macaque presses the shutter of a camera left by David Slater in an Indonesian reserve. Neither the Copyright Office nor the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals recognizes an author for this photo: under American law, only a human being can hold the copyright.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: U.S. Copyright Office, decision on Zarya of the Dawn (February 21, 2023)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The Office refuses protection for AI-generated images within a graphic novel, citing the same human authorship requirement.

quiz.question: Why does the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reject the claim brought by PETA on behalf of the macaque Naruto?
choix: The court rules that David Slater holds the copyright, since he had set up the camera
The court finds that the macaque's act cannot be called creation, for lack of intent
The Copyright Act explicitly confers standing on no animal, even though Naruto suffered a recognized injury
PETA lacked the legal personality needed to represent an animal before a federal court
quiz.explication: The court grants Naruto standing under the Constitution, a concrete injury being alleged, but denies him standing under the Copyright Act, which does not explicitly authorize animals to sue. It does not decide whether Slater, or no one, holds the copyright.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the U.S. Copyright Office state in the edition of its Compendium that took effect on December 22, 2014?
choix: It will now register works produced by animals if a human set up the camera
It will register only works created by a human being, citing a photo taken by a monkey as an example
It requires prior filing with a notary for any photograph taken in the wild
It automatically transfers the copyright to the owner of the equipment used
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Compendium, effective December 22, 2014, states that the Office will register only works created by a human being and cites as its first example a photograph taken by a monkey.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the court of appeals' opinion reveal about the agreement between David Slater and PETA?
choix: An agreement had already been reached seven months earlier, leaving Naruto out of the deal
PETA had withdrawn its suit before the court issued its decision
Slater had handed over all of his copyright to PETA as early as 2011
No agreement was ever reached between the two parties
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In ruling on attorney's fees, Judge Bea notes that an agreement had been reached seven months earlier between Slater and PETA, to which Naruto was not a party; in a separate opinion, Judge N.R. Smith faults PETA for turning him into an instrument of its own cause.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Copyright Office rely on in 2023 to refuse protection for the images in Zarya of the Dawn?
choix: The fact that the work reuses characters already protected by another publisher
A 2022 law specifically banning the use of generative artificial intelligence
The author's refusal to name a single human person responsible for the project
The absence of a human hand behind the result, the same requirement set because of the monkey in 2014
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Office refuses protection for the images in Zarya of the Dawn by relying on the human authorship requirement set nine years earlier because of the monkey: without a human hand behind the result, no one can be named as the author.
